title: Side project with Dana
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex pitches mentor Dana a side-project app that helps museums prototype interactive exhibits and weighs it against taking the studio job; Dana recommends Never Split the Difference for co-founder talks and defers the funding question, which never comes back.

utterances.text: Okay, I have a weird question. What if instead of the studio job, I built something myself?
Oh, interesting. What's the something?
So, an app for museums. You sketch an interactive exhibit, like a touch table or a quiz panel, and test it with visitors on a tablet before anyone builds hardware.
Prototyping for exhibits. Where did this come from?
The studio interviews, actually. They said half their budget goes to building stuff that visitors ignore.
That's a real problem. Who would pay, though? The museums or the studios?
Studios, probably. Small ones like the one that made me the offer.
Okay. So here's the honest version. You've never shipped a product and you've never sold anything.
Ouch. Yeah.
Which is why I'd take the studio job first. You'd be inside the exact customer you're designing for.
So the job is like research for the startup idea?
Paid research. With benefits. You learn how exhibits really get made, and you build the app on weekends if it still feels urgent.
That's less romantic, but it makes sense.
Are you doing this alone?
My friend from school is a developer. She's interested, but we haven't talked about who does what.
Have that conversation early. Remember the book? Never Split the Difference?
Chris Voss. I'm halfway through it.
Use it on her. Not to win, to understand. Ask the open questions. How would you want this to work? What would make you walk away?
The calibrated questions chapter.
Exactly. And label what you hear. It sounds like you're worried about the time commitment. People open up when they feel heard.
I literally just used that on the studio for the salary thing.
Then you know it works. Co-founders split up over unspoken stuff way more than over bad ideas.
Okay. What about money, though? Do I need investors?
Let's talk money another time, that's a whole evening on its own.
Fair. So, studio job, keep the app as a weekend thing, and a real conversation with my friend.
And write down the problem the studio told you about. Exact words. That's your first user interview.
Ha, I didn't even know I was doing user research.
You were. Most good ideas start as a complaint someone made in passing.
